Bank Churn Prediction

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

Businesses like banks which provide service have to worry about problem of 'Customer Churn' i.e. customers leaving and joining another service provider. It is important to understand which aspects of the service influence a customer's decision in this regard. Management can concentrate efforts on improvement of service, keeping in mind these priorities.

Objective¶

You as a Data scientist with the bank need to build a neural network based classifier that can determine whether a customer will leave the bank or not in the next 6 months.

Data Dictionary¶

  • CustomerId: Unique ID which is assigned to each customer

  • Surname: Last name of the customer

  • CreditScore: It defines the credit history of the customer.

  • Geography: A customer’s location

  • Gender: It defines the Gender of the customer

  • Age: Age of the customer

  • Tenure: Number of years for which the customer has been with the bank

  • NumOfProducts: refers to the number of products that a customer has purchased through the bank.

  • Balance: Account balance

  • HasCrCard: It is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer has credit card or not.

  • EstimatedSalary: Estimated salary

  • isActiveMember: Is is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer is active member of the bank or not ( Active member in the sense, using bank products regularly, making transactions etc )

  • Exited : whether or not the customer left the bank within six month. It can take two values ** 0=No ( Customer did not leave the bank ) ** 1=Yes ( Customer left the bank )

The below functions need to be defined to carry out the Exploratory Data Analysis.¶

In [15]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    ax_box2.set_title(f'Boxplot for {feature}')
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
    ax_hist2.set_title(f'Histogram for {feature}')
    # Adjust layout to prevent title overlap
    plt.tight_layout()
In [16]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot
In [17]:
# function to plot stacked bar chart

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.title(f"Distribution of {target} (0 - Exisiting, 1 - Attrited) by {predictor}")
    plt.xlabel(predictor)
    plt.ylabel("Proportion")
    plt.show()
In [18]:
### Function to plot distributions

# This function will be used in bivariant analysis

def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title(f"Distribution of {predictor} for {target}=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title(f"Distribution of {predictor} for {target}=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Univariate Analysis¶

1. CreditScore¶

It defines the credit history of the customer.

In [19]:
# Histogram and boxplot for CreditScore
histogram_boxplot(data, "CreditScore")

Observation¶

  • Distribution

    • The histogram shows a roughly normal distribution with a slight right skew
    • The mean credit score (around 650) is represented by the green triangle in the boxplot
    • There's a notable spike in frequency around credit scores of 850 (maximum score)

  • Key Features

    • Range: 350-850, which is the standard credit score range
    • Median (vertical line in boxplot): approximately 650
    • Interquartile Range (pink box in boxplot): approximately 584-718
    • Several outliers on the lower end (dots in boxplot)

  • Key Observations

    • Most customers have credit scores between 550-750
    • There's a healthy concentration of customers with excellent credit scores (800+)
    • Very few customers have scores below 400

2. Age¶

Age of the customer

In [20]:
# Histogram and boxplot for Age
histogram_boxplot(data, "Age")

Observation¶

  • Distribution

    • Strong positive (right) skew in the age distribution
    • Unimodal with peak concentration around 37-40 years
    • Non-normal distribution with heavy right tail
    • Clear cutoff at 18 years (minimum age for banking)

  • Key Features

    • Range: 18-92 years
    • Median (from boxplot): ~37 years
    • IQR (pink box): ~32-44 years (relatively narrow)
    • Mean (green triangle): ~39 years, slightly higher than median due to right skew
    • Substantial number of outliers above age 60 (dots in boxplot)

  • Key Observations

    • Dominant young-to-middle-age customer base (30-45 years)
    • Sharp decline in customer numbers after age 45
    • Limited representation of customers above 60 years
    • Very few customers in 18-20 age range
    • Notable spikes at certain ages (e.g., around 40, 50, 60) suggesting possible age rounding in data collection

3. Balance¶

Account balance

In [21]:
# Histogram and boxplot for Balance
histogram_boxplot(data, "Balance")

Observation¶

  • Distribution

    • Highly right-skewed distribution
    • Bimodal distribution with two distinct peaks:
      • First peak at 0 (very large number of zero-balance accounts)
      • Second peak around 100,000-125,000
    • Long right tail extending to 250,000
    • Non-normal distribution requiring transformation for modeling

  • Key Features

    • Range: 0-250,898.09
    • Mean (green dashed line): ~76,486
    • Median (solid black line): Lower than mean due to right skew
    • IQR (pink box): Shows high spread in non-zero balances
    • Large number of outliers on the higher end
    • Distinct zero-balance cluster

  • Key Observations

    • Extremely high frequency of zero-balance accounts (~3500 customers)
    • Most non-zero balances fall between 75,000-150,000
    • Relatively few accounts with balances over 200,000
    • Clear gap between zero-balance accounts and the next balance level
    • High variance in account balances suggests diverse customer segments

This distribution will need careful handling in the model:

Need to use normalization techniques on this column. We will apply the technique on all numeric column.

plt.title("Correlation Heatmap")
sns.heatmap(data[numeric_columns].corr(), annot=True, cmap="PiYG", fmt='.2f')
plt.show()

Observation¶

  • Key Correlations with Exited (Churn)

    • Age: Strongest positive correlation (0.29)
    • IsActiveMember: Notable negative correlation (-0.16)
    • Balance: Weak positive correlation (0.12)
    • NumOfProducts: Weak negative correlation (-0.05)
    • Other features show very weak correlations (< |0.05|)

  • Notable Feature Interactions

    • Balance & NumOfProducts: Moderate negative correlation (-0.30)
      • Suggests customers with more products tend to have lower balances
    • Most other feature pairs show very weak correlations (< |0.10|)
    • Almost no correlation between most demographic and behavioral variables

  • Key Observations

    • Overall weak to moderate correlations throughout
    • Age is the strongest predictor of churn
    • Active membership status is a protective factor against churn
    • Many features show independence from each other
    • Multicollinearity is not a major concern as correlations are generally low

Data Preprocessing¶

Outlier Detection¶

In [42]:
# Select only numeric columns
numeric_cols = data.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns
numeric_data = data[numeric_cols]

# Now calculate quantiles
Q1 = numeric_data.quantile(0.25)  # To find the 25th percentile
Q3 = numeric_data.quantile(0.75)  # To find the 75th percentile

IQR = Q3 - Q1  # Inter Quantile Range (75th percentile - 25th percentile)

# Calculate bounds for outliers
lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
In [43]:

# Create distribution data with counts and percentages
def get_distribution(y):
    counts = y.value_counts()
    percentages = y.value_counts(normalize=True)
    combined = pd.DataFrame({
        'Count': counts,
        'Percentage': percentages * 100
    })
    return combined

# Create DataFrames for each set
original_dist = get_distribution(y)
train_dist = get_distribution(y_train)
val_dist = get_distribution(y_val)
test_dist = get_distribution(y_test)

# Add a 'Set' identifier to each DataFrame
original_dist['Set'] = 'Original Set'
train_dist['Set'] = 'Training Set'
val_dist['Set'] = 'Validation Set'
test_dist['Set'] = 'Test Set'

# Concatenate all DataFrames
dist_df = pd.concat([original_dist, train_dist, val_dist, test_dist])

# Reset index to make 'Exited' a column
dist_df = dist_df.reset_index()
dist_df = dist_df.rename(columns={'index': 'Exited'})  # Changed from 'Class' to 'Exited'

# Replace class values with descriptive labels
dist_df['Exited'] = dist_df['Exited'].map({0: 'Non-churned (0)', 1: 'Churned (1)'})

# Format percentages
dist_df['Percentage'] = dist_df['Percentage'].round(1).astype(str) + '%'

# Reorder columns for better presentation
dist_df = dist_df[['Set', 'Exited', 'Count', 'Percentage']]

print("\nDetailed Class Distribution Across Sets:")
print(dist_df.to_string(index=False))

Data Normalization¶

Why data normalization is important, especially for neural networks:

  • Brings all features to similar scale
  • Prevents features with larger values from dominating
  • Helps gradient descent converge faster
  • Reduces the chance of getting stuck in local optima
  • Makes model training more stable

In Our Dataset:

  • Balance: 0 to 250,000
  • Age: 18 to 92
  • CreditScore: 350 to 850
  • EstimatedSalary: 11 to 199,992

Without normalization, Balance would have much more influence than Age simply due to its scale

In [50]:
# Initialize the scaler
scaler = StandardScaler()

# Select only numeric columns for scaling
numeric_columns = ['CreditScore', 'Age', 'Tenure', 'Balance', 'EstimatedSalary']

# StandardScaler transforms features to mean=0 and std=1
# Fit scaler on training data only (to prevent data leakage)
X_train[numeric_columns] = scaler.fit_transform(X_train[numeric_columns])

# Apply same transformation to validation and test sets
# Using parameters learned from training data
X_val[numeric_columns] = scaler.transform(X_val[numeric_columns])
X_test[numeric_columns] = scaler.transform(X_test[numeric_columns])

# Quick check
print("\nMean of scaled features (should be close to 0):")
print(X_train[numeric_columns].mean())
print("\nStd of scaled features (should be close to 1):")
print(X_train[numeric_columns].std())

Model Building¶

Utility Functions¶

In [51]:
def plot(history, name):
    """
    Function to plot loss/accuracy

    history: an object which stores the metrics and losses.
    name: can be one of Loss or Recall
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots() #Creating a subplot with figure and axes.
    plt.plot(history.history[name]) #Plotting the train accuracy or train loss
    plt.plot(history.history['val_'+name]) #Plotting the validation accuracy or validation loss

    plt.title('Model ' + name.capitalize()) #Defining the title of the plot.
    plt.ylabel(name.capitalize()) #Capitalizing the first letter.
    plt.xlabel('Epoch') #Defining the label for the x-axis.
    fig.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc="outside right upper") #Defining the legend, loc controls the position of the legend.
In [52]:
def plot_roc_and_find_optimal_threshold(model, X, y, model_name='Model'):
    """
    Plot ROC curve and find optimal threshold using G-mean

    Parameters:
    model: trained model object
    X: feature matrix
    y: true labels
    model_name: name of the model for plot title (default='Model')

    Returns:
    optimal_threshold: threshold that maximizes G-mean
    g_mean: maximum G-mean value
    """

    # Predicting probabilities
    y_pred_proba = model.predict(X)
    # Keeping probabilities for positive outcomes
    y_pred_proba = y_pred_proba[:, 0]

    # Calculating ROC curve
    fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y, y_pred_proba)

    # Calculating G-mean for each threshold
    gmeans = np.sqrt(tpr * (1-fpr))

    # Finding optimal threshold
    ix = np.argmax(gmeans)
    optimal_threshold = thresholds[ix]
    g_mean = gmeans[ix]

    # Creating plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.plot([0,1], [0,1], linestyle='--', label='No Skill')
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, marker='.', label='ROC curve')
    plt.scatter(fpr[ix], tpr[ix], marker='o', color='black', label=f'Best Threshold={optimal_threshold:.3f}')

    # Customizing plot
    plt.xlabel('False Positive Rate')
    plt.ylabel('True Positive Rate')
    plt.title(f'ROC Curve - {model_name}')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)

    # Print optimal values
    print(f'Best Threshold={optimal_threshold:.3f}, G-Mean={g_mean:.3f}')

    plt.show()

    return optimal_threshold, g_mean

def make_confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets, perf_metric):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    actual_targets: actual target (dependent) variable values
    predicted_targets: predicted target (dependent) variable values
    perf_metric: Has Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score
    """
    cm = confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets)
    categories = ['Non-churned', 'Churned']
    cmap = sns.cm.rocket_r

    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(cm.shape[0], cm.shape[1])

    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap=cmap, xticklabels=categories, yticklabels=categories)

    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

    plt.show()
    print(perf_metric.to_string(index=False))

# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: threshold for classifying the observation as class 1
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors) > threshold

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf, pred

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

  • Correct Predition:

    • True positives (TP) are failures correctly predicted by the model.

  • Types of Wrong Predictions:

    • False Positive (FP): Predicting a customer will churn when they actually won't

      • Business Impact: Unnecessary retention efforts and resources
      • Cost: Additional marketing/retention costs

    • False Negative (FN): Predicting a customer won't churn when they actually will

      • Business Impact: Loss of customer without preventive action
      • Cost: Lost revenue, customer acquisition costs, reputation damage

  • More Critical Case - False Negatives are more costly because:

    • Losing a customer is more expensive than spending on retention
    • Customer acquisition costs are typically higher than retention costs
    • Lost revenue from customer's lifetime value
    • Harder to win back a churned customer

  • Why Recall is Important: Recall (Sensitivity) is indeed crucial because:

    • Recall = TP/(TP + FN)
    • Measures our ability to catch actual churners
    • Higher recall means fewer missed churners
    • Directly addresses the costlier error type

  • Recommended Metrics:

    • Recall: To minimize missed churners
    • ROC-AUC: Overall model discrimination
    • F1-Score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall
    • Confusion Matrix: Detailed error analysis

Loss Function¶

In [61]:
# Plot Loss
plot(history_0, 'loss')

Observatoion

  • Rapid loss decrease in first 10 epochs
  • Gradual convergence after epoch 30
  • Small, consistent gap between training and validation loss
  • Stabilization around epoch 40-50

Recall¶

In [62]:
# Plot Recall
plot(history_0, 'recall')

Observation

  • Initial spike followed by drop to near zero
  • No improvement from epochs 10-30
  • Slow, steady improvement after epoch 30
  • Final recall only reaches ~0.10-0.11 (very poor)

 Accuracy  Recall  Precision  F1 Score

Observation

  • Training Set:

    • High False Negatives (1061, 17.68%)
    • Low True Positives (146, 2.43%)
    • Accuracy: 0.806, Recall: 0.806
    • F1 Score: 0.751

  • Validation Set:

    • Similar pattern of metrics
    • High False Negatives (371, 18.55%)
    • Low True Positives (44, 2.20%)
    • Metrics slightly lower but consistent

  • Key Observation:

    • Model favors predicting non-churners
    • Poor performance in identifying churners
    • Good generalization (similar training/validation)
    • High False Negative rate is concerning for churn prediction

Neural Network with Adam Optimizer¶

Model 1

Model Model 1 - Adam Optimizer
Layers 3 with 66, 33 and neurons respectively
Activation function for Hidden layer ReLU
Activation for output layer Sigmoid
Optimizer Adam
Learning rate 0.001
Loss function binary_crossentropy
Metrics Accuracy, Recall
Epochs 80
Batch Size 48
In [67]:
# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(28)
random.seed(28)
tf.random.set_seed(28)
In [68]:
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
model_1 = Sequential()
# Adding input layer with 66 nodes
# input_dim automatically determined from training data shape
model_1.add(Dense(66, input_dim=X_train.shape[1], activation='relu'))

# Adding hidden layer with 33 nodes (half of previous layer)
# ReLU activation for non-linear transformation
model_1.add(Dense(33, activation='relu'))

# Adding output layer with 1 node for binary classification
# Sigmoid activation to get probability between 0 and 1
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
In [69]:
# Compiling with Adam optimizer and binary cross entropy loss function.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_1.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy', tf.keras.metrics.Recall()])

  • Training/validation divergence indicating overfitting

Neural Network with Adam Optimizer and Dropout¶

Model 2

Model Model 2 - Adam Optimizer and Dropout
Hidden layers 2 with 33 and 16 neurons respectively
Activation function for Hidden layer ReLU
Activation for output layer Sigmoid
Optimizer Adam
Learning rate 0.001
Loss function binary_crossentropy
Metrics Accuracy, Recall
Epochs 80
Batch Size 48
Dropout 20% after before First and Second hidden layer
In [79]:
# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(28)
random.seed(28)
tf.random.set_seed(28)
In [80]:
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
model_2 = Sequential()

# Adding input layer with 66 nodes (6x number of features)
# input_dim automatically determined from training data shape
model_2.add(Dense(66, activation='relu', input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))

# Add dropout layer to prevent overfitting (20% dropout rate)
model_2.add(Dropout(0.2))

# First hidden layer with 33 nodes (half of previous layer)
model_2.add(Dense(33, activation='relu'))

# Another dropout layer for regularization
model_2.add(Dropout(0.2))

# Second hidden layer with 16 nodes (~half of previous layer)
model_2.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))

# Output layer with sigmoid activation for binary classification
# Single node outputs probability between 0 and 1
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
In [81]:
# Compiling with Adam optimizer and binary cross entropy loss function.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_2.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy', tf.keras.metrics.Recall()])

model_2.summary()

Loss Function¶

In [84]:
# Plot Loss
plot(history_2, 'loss')

Observation

  • Sharp initial loss decrease (0-10 epochs)
  • Growing gap between training/validation after epoch 20
  • Training loss continues declining
  • Validation loss plateaus ~0.38 with slight increase
  • Best validation performance around epoch 20
  • Signs of overfitting after epoch 20
  • Validation loss becomes unstable (small oscillations)

Recall¶

In [85]:
# Plot Recall
plot(history_2, 'recall')

Observation

  • Quick recall improvement until epoch 20
  • Training recall stabilizes ~0.50-0.52
  • Validation recall peaks early then declines to ~0.45
  • Oscillating behavior in both curves
  • Best validation recall around epoch 20-25

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and SGD Optimizer¶

Let's try to apply SMOTE to balance this dataset and then again apply hyperparamter tuning accordingly.

In [91]:
# SMOTE to balance this dataset
smote = SMOTE(random_state=28)
X_train_smote, y_train_smote = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)
print('Original shape of train_X: {}'.format(X_train.shape))
print('Original shape of train_y: {} \n'.format(y_train.shape))
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_X: {}'.format(X_train_smote.shape))
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_y: {} \n'.format(y_train_smote.shape))

Original shape of train_X: (6000, 11)
Original shape of train_y: (6000,) 

After UpSampling, the shape of train_X: (9586, 11)
After UpSampling, the shape of train_y: (9586,)

Model 3

Model Model 3 - SGD Optimizer (Balanced dataset)
Hidden layers 2 with 33 and 16 neurons respectively
Activation function for Hidden layer ReLU
Activation for output layer Sigmoid
Optimizer SGD
Learning rate 0.001
Loss function binary_crossentropy
Metrics Accuracy, Recall
Epochs 80
Batch Size 48
In [92]:
# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(28)
random.seed(28)
tf.random.set_seed(28)
In [93]:
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
model_3 = Sequential()
# Adding input layer with 66 nodes (6x number of features)
# input_dim automatically determined from training data shape
model_3.add(Dense(66, activation='relu', input_dim=X_train_smote.shape[1]))

# First hidden layer with 33 nodes (half of previous layer)
model_3.add(Dense(33, activation='relu'))

# Second hidden layer with 16 nodes (~half of previous layer)
model_3.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))

# Output layer with sigmoid activation for binary classification
# Single node outputs probability between 0 and 1
model_3.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
In [94]:
# Compiling with SGD optimizer and binary cross entropy loss function.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.001)
model_3.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy', tf.keras.metrics.Recall()])

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and Adam Optimizer¶

Model 4

Model Model 4 - Adam Optimizer (Balanced dataset)
Hidden layers 2 with 33 and 16 neurons respectively
Activation function for Hidden layer ReLU
Activation for output layer Sigmoid
Optimizer Adam
Learning rate 0.001
Loss function binary_crossentropy
Metrics Accuracy, Recall
Epochs 80
Batch Size 48
In [104]:
# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(28)
random.seed(28)
tf.random.set_seed(28)
In [105]:
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
model_4 = Sequential()
# Adding input layer with 66 nodes (6x number of features)
# input_dim automatically determined from training data shape
model_4.add(Dense(66, activation='relu', input_dim=X_train_smote.shape[1]))

# First hidden layer with 33 nodes (half of previous layer)
model_4.add(Dense(33, activation='relu'))

# Second hidden layer with 16 nodes (~half of previous layer)
model_4.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))

# Output layer with sigmoid activation for binary classification
# Single node outputs probability between 0 and 1
model_4.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
In [106]:
# Compiling with Adam optimizer and binary cross entropy loss function.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_4.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy', tf.keras.metrics.Recall()])

Loss Function¶

In [109]:
# Plot Loss
plot(history_4, 'loss')

Observation

  • Training loss steadily decreases
  • Validation loss increases significantly after epoch 20
  • Large and growing gap between curves
  • Clear sign of severe overfitting

Recall¶

In [110]:
# Plot Recall
plot(history_4, 'recall')

Observation

  • Training recall keeps improving to ~0.95
  • Validation recall declines steadily after epoch 10
  • Large gap between training/validation recalls
  • Severe overfitting pattern

Observation

  • Training Set:

    • True Negatives: 4421 (46.12%)
    • True Positives: 4535 (47.76%)
    • Exceptional metrics: Accuracy/Recall/F1 all ~0.933

  • Validation Set:

    • True Negatives: 1349 (67.45%)
    • True Positives: 231 (11.55%)
    • Much lower metrics: Accuracy 0.790, F1 0.794

  • Key Observation:

    • Major overfitting evident
    • Large performance drop in validation
    • Training performance unrealistically high
    • Poor generalization to new data

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE), Adam Optimizer, and Dropout¶

Model 5

Model Model 5 - Adam Optimizer with Dropout (Balenced)
Hidden layers 2 with 66 and 33 neurons respectively
Activation function for Hidden layer ReLU
Activation for output layer Sigmoid
Optimizer Adam
Learning rate 0.001
Loss function binary_crossentropy
Metrics Accuracy, Recall

# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(28)
random.seed(28)
tf.random.set_seed(28)
In [117]:
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
# Initialize the Sequential Neural Network
model_5 = Sequential()

# Adding input layer with 66 nodes (6x number of features)
# input_dim automatically determined from training data shape
model_5.add(Dense(66, activation='relu', input_dim=X_train_smote.shape[1]))

# Add dropout layer to prevent overfitting (20% dropout rate)
model_5.add(Dropout(0.2))

# First hidden layer with 33 nodes (half of previous layer)
model_5.add(Dense(33, activation='relu'))

# Another dropout layer for regularization
model_5.add(Dropout(0.2))

# Second hidden layer with 16 nodes (~half of previous layer)
model_5.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))

# Output layer with sigmoid activation for binary classification
# Single node outputs probability between 0 and 1
model_5.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
In [118]:
# Compiling with Adam optimizer and binary cross entropy loss function.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_5.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss='binary_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy', tf.keras.metrics.Recall()])

Observation

  • Best Overall Model: ANN Adam - Dropout [0.2,0.2]
    • Training: Accuracy 0.888, Recall 0.888, F1 0.883
    • Validation: Accuracy 0.842, Recall 0.842, F1 0.832
    • Best balance between performance and generalization
    • Minimal overfitting compared to other models

Model Comparisons:

  • Basic Models (No Regularization):
    • SGD performs worst
    • Adam shows improvement but overfits
  • SMOTE Models:
    • Improved recall but lower overall metrics
    • More balanced predictions
  • Dropout Models:
    • Best validation performance
    • Good generalization
    • Most stable metrics

Recommendations:

Use ANN Adam with Dropout as final model

The dropout model provides the best combination of high performance and good generalization.

Let's check the performance of Adam with Dropout on test data

  • Key Observations:
    • Strong balanced performance across all metrics
    • Low false positive rate is good for targeted retention efforts
    • False negatives still need attention
    • High accuracy in identifying non-churners
    • Reasonable performance in identifying churners

This model shows solid performance with balanced metrics, making it reliable for churn prediction tasks.

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

Actionable Insights

  • Older customers (45-60 years) have higher churn risk
  • Young customers (20-35) show better retention
  • Need age-specific retention strategies
  • Germany has highest churn rate (32.4%)
  • France and Spain show better retention (~16.7%)
  • Two products is optimal (lowest churn - 7.6%)
  • Three or more products show very high churn (>80%)
  • Female customers show higher churn rates

Business Recommendatations

  • Develop personalized retention programs for older customers

  • Create targeted engagement programs for inactive members

  • Focus on optimizing two-product combinations

  • Conduct detailed market analysis in Germany

  • Apply successful practices from France/Spain to German market

  • Investigate and address female customer pain points

  • Enhance product education and support for older customers

  • Review service quality in German market

Power Ahead
